children.text: Travelling from Japan to Egypt is a long-distance trip. It is not a hard trip. The question is not "can I go" — it is which season, which flight route, and where to spend the limited days.
Egypt is strong even for a first visit. The
Giza
pyramids, the temples of
Luxor
, the Nile at
Aswan
Abu Simbel

, the Red Sea. Even the names you already know are enough to support a trip. Rushed together, the impression thins. Coming from Japan, where the transfer takes real time, the value on the ground is less "seeing more" and more "ordering what you see."
How to think about the flight route
From Japan to Egypt, when timing aligns, a direct flight links Tokyo-Narita and
Cairo
. A direct flight makes the trip considerably easier. No connection wait, easier-to-read arrival fatigue, a more stable first day.

Depending on your Japanese departure city and dates, connecting flights are often the more realistic choice. Middle-Eastern and Turkish routes via Dubai, Doha, or Istanbul work well from Kansai, Chubu, and Fukuoka, and they sometimes let you target arrival cities other than Cairo.

For a first Egypt trip, the standard doorway is Cairo. Seeing Giza, Saqqara, the museums, the Islamic quarter, and the Coptic quarter, then heading south, makes the layers of Egyptian time connect naturally. If the Red Sea is the main goal, connections to Sharm el-Sheikh,
Hurghada
, or
Marsa Alam
become candidates; for a first cultural trip, entering through Cairo gives you the bigger picture more easily.

When comparing flights, don't decide on total flight time alone. Late-night arrivals, long connections, and early-morning domestic connections all shape the first day heavily. On the arrival day, don't pack it; build the trip so that real movement starts the next morning.
Visa and entry

Japanese passport holders need a visa for Egypt for tourism, either before departure or on arrival. Visa on arrival and the e-visa system can be used at certain airports; the conditions, fees, and eligible airports change. Before travelling, check Egypt's official e-visa site and Japan's MOFA travel safety information.

Passport residual validity matters at entry. The airline checks at check-in too, so don't cut the remaining validity close. Travel insurance is not formality reassurance; for the actual transfer distances, it should be taken. Egyptian inter-city movement is long, with domestic flights, road transfers, boats, and desert routes appearing in itineraries.
When to go

The easiest window from Japan is October to April. Days move comfortably and the sites in Cairo, Luxor, and Aswan all work. November, February, and March balance climate and crowds and suit first trips.

December to January is comfortable and high season. Hotels, cruises, guides, and domestic flights need to be locked in early. From May onward, temperatures rise; in Luxor and Aswan, daytime sightseeing wants stamina. Summer trips are possible — design around early-morning movement and midday rest.

The Red Sea is slightly different. For a diving or snorkelling priority, season thinking differs from Cairo and Luxor. Winter water cools; for long sessions, a wetsuit is realistic. Summer works as a sea trip; loading it like a sightseeing trip wears you out.
How many days
From Japan, want at least eight to ten days in Egypt itself. Given the flight time, five or six is not impossible, but you'll end at Giza and Cairo or rush the south.

For a first trip, ten to twelve days is the most stable. Two or three nights in Cairo and Giza, two in Luxor, two in Aswan, a Nile cruise inserted if needed, return to Cairo. Add the Red Sea and twelve to fourteen days makes it sit without strain.

With two weeks, Egypt reads very differently. Giza and Saqqara, Luxor east and west banks, Aswan, Abu Simbel, time on the Nile, and rest on the Red Sea can be separated cleanly. For a long-distance Japan trip, adding days is less luxury and more the way to recover transfer fatigue inside the trip.
What to see in Cairo and Giza

Once in Cairo, don't end with just the Giza pyramids. Giza is strong; it is not Egypt's beginning. Add the step pyramid at Saqqara, the Pyramid Texts inside Unas, and the memory of Memphis nearby, and the pyramid stops looking like a sudden miracle — it reads as the result of long experiment.

The Grand Egyptian Museum makes the Giza stay weightier than before. Tutankhamun's funerary equipment, dynastic art, colossal sculpture — all close to the pyramids. The Egyptian Museum on Tahrir Square also matters, tied to modern Cairo's history. With time, both are worth seeing.

Don't drop the Islamic and Coptic quarters too far on a first trip. Egypt is not only pharaonic. Mosques, churches, alleys, markets, and the urban memory from the nineteenth century onward layer to make current Cairo. For travellers from Japan, the density of this present city sometimes stays as strongly as the ancient sites.
Luxor and Aswan
Luxor is the centre of an Egypt trip. If Cairo is the doorway, Luxor is the depth. Karnak,
Luxor Temple
, the
Valley of the Kings
, Hatshepsut,
Medinet Habu
. Listing the names is easy; on the ground, the east and west banks play different roles. The east bank is the living temple city. The west bank is the landscape of death and rebirth.

In the Valley of the Kings, rather than counting tombs entered, choose what to see. Tutankhamun, Seti I, Ramses V and VI often require separate tickets, and adding everything is not the point. Decide priorities by preservation, crowding, stamina, and heat.
Aswan is quieter than Luxor. Philae,
the Unfinished Obelisk

, the Nile islands, Nubian culture, and Aswan as the gateway to Abu Simbel. Abu Simbel is far; reaching it earns its place. Not only the rock-cut temple itself but the modern story of the 1960s UNESCO relocation makes this site particular.
Whether to include a Nile cruise
For travellers from Japan, a Nile cruise combines transfer and sightseeing usefully. Moving by boat between Luxor and Aswan, you stop at
Edfu
and
Kom Ombo
. Not changing hotels each day stabilises the schedule.

Large cruises are efficient; their movement is fixed. Disembarkation times, sightseeing windows, and meal times follow the boat's rhythm. They suit short trips; they are not exactly the trip of looking quietly at the river.

For a slower Nile, a dahabiya is the option. Smaller sailing-style cruises take more time and, depending on the boat, include smaller villages and quieter moorings. Higher price, fewer cabins; for travellers who want to change the speed of seeing Egypt, it fits.
If you add the Red Sea
The Red Sea works well at the end of the trip. After Cairo, Luxor, and Aswan in stone and history, restore the body on the water. For long-distance trips from Japan, this is a reasonable shape.

Sharm el-Sheikh is the Sinai-side resort, strong for Ras Mohammed and Strait of Tiran diving. Hurghada is the major west-coast Red Sea base, easy to combine with Luxor. Marsa Alam is further south and suits travellers focused on the sea itself.
A single Red Sea night is mostly transfer load. To add the sea, at least two nights, ideally three, gives meaningful rest.
Japanese-language guides and the feel of the trip
Japanese-speaking guides can be arranged in Cairo, Giza, Luxor, and Aswan. Numbers are limited. Around New Year, cherry-blossom-period Japanese holidays, and Egypt's peak season, arrange early.

You can travel with an English-speaking guide; explanation changes the impression of Egyptian sites significantly. Hieroglyphs, gods, royal names, the orientation of architecture, the difference between a tomb and a temple are hard to read on sight alone. For deep understanding in Japanese, treat guide quality as a central condition.

Culturally, Egypt is more direct than Japan, with more bargaining and tipping. That is not rudeness — society moves differently. Hotels, drivers, boats, site attendants, and restaurants all involve small cash. You don't need to fear every step; planning to avoid tipping entirely makes the trip more tiring.

For dress, prioritise mobility at sites and modesty at religious sites. At mosques and churches, don't expose shoulders or knees significantly. Desert and sites see strong sun — hat, sunglasses, walking shoes are needed. Cairo nights and the boat deck in winter can be cold.
Safety and checks

Egypt's main tourist destinations are visited by many travellers. Cairo, Giza, Luxor, Aswan, and the Red Sea resorts are standard tourism routes. Border areas, North Sinai, and parts of the desert have different status — check Japan's MOFA safety information before travelling.

In-city movement is stable with trusted transfers, hotel arrangements, and ride-hailing. For long-distance transfers, desert routes, and night moves, don't choose on price alone. On an Egypt trip, the quality of local arrangements maps directly to the experience.

Don't drink tap water; use bottled. For those with sensitive stomachs, be cautious with ice, raw vegetables, and street food. Bring needed medicines from Japan; with pre-existing conditions, carry English prescription information.
Why the trip is worth it from Japan

Japan and Egypt are both countries that carry long time. How that time appears is completely different. In Japan, old things often survive quietly inside daily life. In Egypt, kings, gods, the dead, the river, and the desert appear in front of you on a startlingly large scale.

That is exactly why a Japan-to-Egypt trip is better not rushed. To see only the pyramids, you can shorten the trip. Cairo to Luxor, Luxor to Aswan, and on to the Red Sea if you can — and Egypt turns from a "country of famous sites" into a country that travels time itself.
The distance from Japan is real. To cross it, give the itinerary the same kind of margin.

deck: A practical guide for travellers planning Egypt from Japan — flights, entry, season, days, and the order in which to visit.
